item.title: Workstation pricing resets on January 1
item.description:
In this issue

  • Every price action that took effect in October, and what landed as published
  • Lenovo’s January 1 ThinkStation increase and the GPU costs behind it
  • The effective dates and order deadlines already published through January 2027
  • One planning move: get more from the devices you already own before you buy

The month in brief

October was the month the fall increases took hold

Seven price actions took effect between October 1 and October 5: Microsoft Surface, HP Carepack services, Lenovo Top Seller, Panasonic TOUGHBOOK, and Ericsson on October 1, then Zebra and Elo on October 5. Each landed as published, with no revision received. The increases now reach well past PCs into services, rugged devices, scanners, and network hardware.

New notices slowed to one, and it points at 2027. On October 19 Lenovo told partners that ThinkStation prices rise significantly on January 1, 2027, driven by NVIDIA GPU cost increases of 17-74%, with memory and SSD costs expected to follow. Orders that ship in January will be repriced. Dell has indicated a 10-20% increase in early November, the start of its fiscal fourth quarter, and Samsung’s S and Z series move November 1.

Price actions in October 2026

Source: manufacturer and distribution partner communications

Fig. 1 · The calendar ahead

Order deadlines and effective dates · Nov 1 – Jan 1

The deadline that matters is the ship date

Fig. 2 · How often it landed

Price actions by manufacturer · Dec 2025 → Jan 2027

33 pricing actions have been in effect since December 2025. Four more are on the calendar: Samsung S and Z series on November 1, Dell (+10-20% expected) in early November, HP (expected) in November, and Lenovo ThinkStation on January 1, 2027. Actions with a published effective date are shown; December-July totals were reported in prior issues.

Effective dates ahead

What is already on the calendar

Nov 1 · Samsung Galaxy S and Z series. Increases of up to $200 on the S series and up to $300 on the Z series, following the September A-series move. Samsung said further detail would follow once confirmed and that all pricing remains subject to change. No further notice had been received at press time.

The move: Requote open flagship handset orders at the new MSRP before they go to a stakeholder.

November · Dell and HP client devices, expected. Dell has indicated a 10-20% increase in early November, the start of its fiscal fourth quarter. Channel briefings in September pointed to a further 10-15% move on HP client devices in HP’s first fiscal quarter. Neither had issued a written notice at press time.

The move: Place Dell orders that are ready now, before the early-November increase, and keep current HP quotes short.

Dec 31 · Two price locks expire with the year. Lenovo honors current ThinkStation pricing only for orders that ship by December 31 from available-to-sell or distribution inventory. Ericsson honors current MSRP for non-cancellable orders accepted by October 1, but only for quantities delivered and billed by December 31.

The move: Check delivery and billing dates on every open Ericsson order, and confirm which ThinkStation configurations are on available-to-sell inventory now.

Jan 1, 2027 · Lenovo ThinkStation increase. Lenovo calls the increase significant but has not published a percentage. Backlog that rolls into January will be repriced, and configurations not on available-to-sell inventory should be quoted at next quarter’s costs.

The move: Quote 2027 workstation needs at next quarter’s costs now, so the budget carries the real number.

Supply signals

The cost driver has moved up the bill of materials.

Lenovo tied its ThinkStation increase to NVIDIA GPU costs rising 17-74%, with memory and SSD storage expected to rise further. That follows HP’s August briefing, which put processors and graphics cards up roughly 30% and said the trend would carry into 2027. Workstations carry the most GPU and memory content per unit, so they are the most exposed.

Terms keep tightening around each increase. Lenovo will not honor current pricing for backlog that slips into January, Panasonic prices on requested delivery date rather than order date, and Ericsson’s protection depends on delivery and billing by December 31. The deadline that matters is now the ship date, not the order date.

74%: the top of the NVIDIA GPU cost increase range Lenovo cited in its October 19 ThinkStation notice. Reported through October 28, 2026.

One planning move

Before you buy, look at what you already own

The increases that raise the price of a new device also raise the value of every device already in service. Each one that stays productive for another year is one you do not have to buy at next year’s price, which makes the installed fleet the first place to look before the next order.

Redeploy first. Returned and idle devices belong in a central pool, not on the shelf of the last team that used them. A device that matches most of the fleet can go to almost any open role.

Upgrade where the hardware allows it. Desktops and workstations with removable memory and storage can often take modules recovered from units being retired, which matters more now that memory is driving the increases. Many thin laptops solder memory to the board, and warranty terms for added memory vary by manufacturer, so check both before planning around it.

Recover value sooner. A retired device loses resale value every month it sits in storage. Start returns when notice is given, not on the last day.

Buy what must be new before it reprices. Dell client pricing is expected to rise 10-20% in early November, so Dell orders that are ready should go in now. For the GPU workstations and network hardware the fleet cannot supply, two price locks end with the year. Lenovo honors current ThinkStation pricing only for orders that ship by December 31, and Ericsson holds current MSRP for orders accepted by October 1 only if they are delivered and billed by then.

For the longer view on building a second life into every purchase, read Buying for a Circular Economy.

Source note

Pricing actions reflect manufacturer and distribution partner communications tracked by MCPC partner management through October 28, 2026. Individual results vary by configuration, volume, and contract terms. Figures described as reported reflect channel communications rather than published manufacturer price lists. Actions whose effective date passed without a revision notice are reported as published, no revision received. MCPC is a device lifecycle management company headquartered in Cleveland, Ohio.

To view the full November report, visit here.

item.title: Mitigate memory price increases with components harvested from retiring devices
item.description:
The circular economy just picked up one of its strongest business cases yet, and it didn’t come from a sustainability mandate. It came from a memory shortage. An AI-induced memory shortage has pushed the price of new devices up, causing organizations to recalculate their repair-vs-replace threshold, and to look again at what a decommissioned device is still worth.

Rather than proceeding with typical 3 to 4-year refresh cycles, many IT and procurement teams have shifted to preservation mode, holding devices longer where they can and stretching the cycle. Another trend gaining ground: internal component harvesting. Instead of treating retiring or broken laptops as something to dispose of, forward-thinking organizations are treating them as sub-component mines. This means pulling the working memory and graphics cards out of a device too old to redeploy, and putting them into devices that can.

Procurement can buy memory at the new price, or pull it from a device it just decommissioned. The rest of this article covers the three main steps that make the second option work.

First, get the devices back

Recovered devices are the harvesting supply, so the first thing to know is your recovery rate, which is how many devices you can count on getting back, and when.

To accurately measure your recovery rate, you need to track three things:

  • The eligible pool
  • The return rate
  • The yield

The eligible pool is every device that should be coming back in a given window. A device enters the pool for one of four reasons:

  • A scheduled refresh or lease end. These are the most predictable returns, because every device has a date. The purchase or deployment date in the asset record, plus the refresh policy, gives the refresh date. The lease contract gives the lease end. Most asset management systems can produce that list on demand, so count every device whose date falls inside the window. Lease returns carry penalties for late or missing devices, so they tend to be the best-tracked group already.
  • An employee departure. HR’s exit list is the trigger, and the asset record says which device that person holds. The device is due back on their last day or within the return window that follows. Remote departures are where most returns go wrong, so note the person’s location and how the device will travel.
  • A role change that comes with a different device. A move into a role with a different device class, such as a field role that needs a lighter laptop or an engineering role that needs a workstation, puts the old device in the pool. It’s the easiest trigger to miss because nobody leaves. The request that issued the new device is the record to count from.
  • A break/fix swap where a replacement went out and the failed device is owed back. The service desk ticket is the record. A failed device still belongs in the pool as a harvest candidate, because a cracked screen or a dead keyboard says nothing about the memory inside it.

To count the pool, pull the numbers from the systems that already track those events: the asset record and refresh policy, HR’s list of departures and role changes, and the service desk’s record of swaps.

There will always be exceptions, and checking device management tools, such as Intune or Jamf, for devices that haven’t checked in for 30 to 60 days may help locate a few more for the pool.

The return rate is the percentage of the eligible pool that actually came back:

Return rate = devices received ÷ eligible pool × 100

For example, if 100 devices were due back this quarter and 80 were scanned into inventory, the return rate is 80%. A device only counts as received once it’s scanned in, not when the return label is printed.

Two more numbers belong next to the return rate:

  • Days to return. How long each device took to come back, from the day it entered the pool to the day it was scanned in. This is dwell time. Average it, and also count how many came back inside your target window, because a few very late returns can hide inside an average.
  • Leakage rate. The percentage of the pool that didn’t come back at all. Keep two counts: devices still outstanding when the window closes, which may yet arrive, and devices written off, which won’t. Remote workers who miss return windows are the usual cause.

Track all three by reason. A departing employee’s laptop and a swapped one rarely move at the same pace, and a lease return with a penalty behind it moves faster than either.

The yield is the percentage of returned devices that turn out to be usable, either as a device that goes back to a user or as a donor of working parts:

Yield = usable devices ÷ devices received × 100

Of the 80 devices that came back in the example above, if 60 can be redeployed or harvested, the yield is 75%. Physical possession doesn’t automatically equal usable supply, and the next section covers how to set the standard that decides it.

Put the three together and you have the forecast:

Forecast = eligible pool × return rate × yield

In the example, 100 devices due back, at an 80% return rate and a 75% yield, is 60 usable devices. Once that number is known, devices in transit can be treated as inventory. If ten devices are due back within the usual window, that’s ten candidates for harvest, and a request to buy memory at the new price can wait until they’ve been sorted. The forecast only works as the official timeline if purchasing decisions and return tracking both treat it that way. That timeline only holds if the return stays open until the old device is received. A return closed when the replacement ships leaves the old device untracked in a drawer, and out of the count.

Next, decide which devices give and which keep going

Every device that comes back from the field ultimately lands in one of three distinct outcomes: it goes back to a user, it gives up its parts, or it leaves the organization entirely. The first two are what the yield counts. To route every device to the correct outcome, run two checks in order:

Does the device still meet the standard for redeployment?

To pass, it typically needs to satisfy four rules: how old the device can be, measured in processor generations behind the current one; how much memory it has to have, such as 16 GB; what condition it has to be in; and whether any repair costs less than the device is worth. A device that passes all four goes back to a user. One that passes but is close to the age limit usually isn’t worth redeploying. Imaging, shipping and another handoff cost more than the few months it would give, so it moves to the second check.

Does the device hold what in-service devices need?

A device too old to redeploy often carries the same memory and graphics cards a newer device would take, and memory is the part whose price just went up. Suppose the redeployment standard is 16 GB of memory. A device with 8 GB won’t go back to a user, but its memory can go into one that will. A healthcare client’s radiology workstations are the same case: too old for a new user, with working memory and graphics cards inside.

Running the second check means knowing what’s inside each device, which most asset records don’t say. The part number does: it says what the device was built with, and a provider that handles ITAD will usually know the configuration from that before the device is opened. The erasure tool used on a retiring device adds a triage report that lists each component and whether it still works. Record memory and graphics configuration per device from those two sources, and a retiring device can be matched to the in-service devices that need its parts.

A device that fails both checks exits: sold if a secondary buyer will pay for it, recycled if not. In the example from the first section, the 60 usable devices out of 80 received are the ones that passed one of the two checks, and the other 20 are the ones that exited.

Finally, pull the parts and put them to work

A device that failed the first check and passed the second is a donor. Turning it into savings takes three steps:

Pull and test. The memory and graphics cards come out, get tested beyond what the triage report says, and go into storage until a device needs them. This is the step organizations usually need help with, because safe removal, testing and storage take equipment and handling few keep in-house. MCPC does this work inside IT asset disposition (ITAD), the processing of devices leaving an organization, and uses the recovered memory and graphics cards to extend in-service devices that would otherwise have been refreshed.

Match and install. The configuration record from the second check says which in-service devices need what the donor gave up. Memory is the simplest part to match. Graphics cards and the accessories around a device carry more of the compatibility work. A device that receives a donor’s memory stays in service past the refresh date it would otherwise have hit.

Count the savings. A harvested part shows up in a budget as a purchase that didn’t happen, which is harder to see than one that did, so count it:

Cost avoided = harvested parts installed × price of the same part new

Add reclaimed devices at their original purchase price. In the example, if 20 of the 60 usable devices were donors, that’s 20 memory purchases at the new price that didn’t happen, and the number that tells leadership a request was filled from stock the organization already owned. The savings only show up if reclaimed stock is used first. A new request should go to the shelf before it goes to a purchase order.

What’s left of a donor still has a resale value, lower than it had whole. The time to price it is before the refresh decision, not after. A provider with its own ITAD operation can take an inventory list and come back with the resale value and the credit it would produce, which turns the decision from a guess into a comparison. How that value comes back matters. A check goes to central finance and registers as a small line in a large budget. A credit applied to services stays with the budget owner, with no requisition or purchase order to get through.

One thing to know about whoever handles your retiring devices: a disposal vendor earns when a device sells, so its incentive favors selling the device whole over pulling parts from it. A single question shows how a current provider treats this: when a retiring device holds working memory that could extend one of ours, what happens to it, and does the sale of the device affect that choice?

Whether to sell a device whole, recycle it, or harvest it is a finance decision, and it needs three numbers side by side: what the device earns sold whole, what it earns recycled, and what its harvested parts save against new purchases.

How MCPC does this

MCPC runs this process end to end for clients, and has for some time. It starts with the return. MCPC handles the logistics of getting a device back from a user, tracks every return as an open item until the device is scanned in, and reports dwell time against each client’s average so an overdue return stands out before the window closes.

Each client has a routing guide, written with MCPC, that sets the generation limit, the memory minimum, the condition standard and the repair threshold. When a device arrives, MCPC already knows its configuration from the part number, and the erasure process produces a triage report on whether each component works. The device goes to redeployment, harvest or exit on that basis, the same way every time.

Harvesting happens inside MCPC’s ITAD operation. Working memory and graphics cards are pulled, tested, stored and categorized, then matched to in-service devices in the client’s fleet that need them, with compatibility checked before anything ships. Devices that redeploy go back out as complete kits, with the power supply, cables and webcam matched to the device class, because a laptop without its charger does nobody any good.

Before a refresh decision, MCPC prices the client’s retiring inventory through its ITAD facility and shows what it would return as resale value, and what that would be as a credit against services. Reclaimed inventory is used first: when a new request comes in, MCPC’s client success and operations teams fill it from the client’s reclaimed stock before anything is bought. Every reclaimed device is reported at its original purchase price, so the client can show leadership the cost that was avoided, quarter by quarter.

For some clients the program pays for itself. The credits earned by remarketing retiring devices cover the cost of the services, so the harvested memory, the redeployed devices and the purchases that never happened come on top. One client has called it the most effective procurement hedge in their program, and it was built rather than bought.

If your organization is planning its device budget around memory prices, MCPC’s guide to the memory shortage, Corporate Memory Loss: A Practical Guide to Navigating AI-Driven Memory Constraints and Device Strategy, is a place to start. If you’d like to work through your own redeployment standard and donor rules with someone, we’d welcome the conversation, and you can talk with an expert here.

item.title: Uber’s Legal AI Agent Cuts Contract Review Time by 20% with Rules and RAG
item.description:
Uber’s Legal Redlining Agent reviews contract changes in Microsoft Word using RAG, historical lawyer feedback, and deterministic policy rules. Built with LangGraph, OpenSearch, and Redis, the system reports more than 20% lower average contract review time and 91% accuracy in AI-generated decisions. Uber is exploring agentic harnesses, skills, legal ontologies, and knowledge graphs.

By Leela Kumili

item.title: Airbnb Introduces CASTLE for Training Natural Language Search Models with Synthetic Data
item.description:
Airbnb researchers have introduced CASTLE, a framework designed to address the cold-start problem in natural language search. The approach uses de-identified booking sessions and large language models (LLMs) to jointly generate synthetic search queries and relevance labels, enabling model training before sufficient real search traffic is available.

By Robert Krzaczyński

item.title: AWS Open-Sources Emulator for Local Testing of 200+ Services by Coding Agents
item.description:
AWS Emulator is a generally available local HTTPS endpoint, generated from public Smithy API models, that lets developers and coding agents test against more than 200 AWS services without an account, with published fidelity scores and documented limits around IAM, regions, and in-memory state.

By Daniel Dominguez

item.title: IT leaders rethink ‘Big T’ transformation for a new era
item.description:
Longtime IT executive Mohan Sankararaman has transformed how he views transformations.

Sankararaman, CIO of First Horizon, used to run transformations as monumental multiyear IT programs. Today, his transformations are smaller — yet still consequential — changes to how work gets done.

“The definition of ‘transformation’ has changed,” he says. “Ten years ago, it was a large program for IT transformation, where you defined a target state, defined a program with projects under it, and started a two- to three-year initiative you’d execute. But in today’s world, there is not a start and stop point. It’s an ongoing journey that never ends. It’s all about continually changing and building an organization that can adapt and reinvent itself continuously.”

It’s a needed shift, Sankararaman says.

The big transformations in the past focused on implementing new technologies, with success typically measured using IT-type metrics, he explains. Cloud migrations are an illustrative case, with progress and success measured by how many apps IT moved to the cloud and how many were in line for the move.

Compare that with the smaller, more nimble transformations of today where IT and the business use technology — most often AI — to reimagine a single workflow within a larger business process to deliver a desired business outcome, such as improved time to market, which is the measure of success. And then it’s about reengineering another and then another workflow in that process to continuously improve that desired business outcome, he explains.

Linking incremental transformations to bigger outcomes

Sankararaman has persuasive reasons for his updated perspectives on transformation. Topping the list is the increasing pace of change, both in technology (and AI specifically) and in the business environment.

“If you have a two- or three-year big transformation program, when you’re done the outcomes are stale because AI is moving forward in monthly increments,” he says, adding that “three years is a very long time in AI think.”

Smaller, incremental transformations also allow for easier course-correction, he says.

And they better leverage domain expertise in their planning and execution, because business users are teaming with IT to reimagine the tasks they do in their daily work rather than weighing in on companywide processes.

Sankararaman points to his current transformation efforts around loan origination, a critical business process for every bank, to justify his faith in the value of small ‘t’ transformation.

“I could say I want to engineer this whole thing, and it would take 24 months. But it’s made up of multiple sub-workflows, so we’re looking at each sub-workflow and reimagining it,” he says.

That approach brings more agility, he says, not only for course-correction but also to seize on evolving technologies, to adapt to changing business needs, and to ensure adoption of new processes and tools along the way.

Sankararaman stresses that his focus on sub-workflows isn’t about small tweaks and minor changes, because they’re all done in service of the larger objective of transforming the business. “We’re doing smaller items, incremental things, but still continuing that journey to a bigger goal,” he says. “Small things linked together very nicely achieve a bigger outcome.”

Redefining ‘transformation’ as change accelerates

Julie Averill, former EVP and global CIO of Lululemon and now CEO of Gold Thread and author of the book Chief Impact Officer, believes such updated perspectives on transformation are needed.

“It’s a super important topic right now because we’ve all been bedazzled by the word ‘transformation,’” she explains.

“We need to change, because thinking about transformation with a capital ‘T’ implies that it’s a program with a start and end date, that you can bring in consultants to help lead it, and that you can put together a project plan that addresses needs,” she says. “But the pace of business has changed, it has gone up tremendously, so now we need not a transformational program but continuous change. That’s transformation with a little ‘t,’ which means iteration and which brings more speed to change, teams who are close to the business, and continuous learning.”

Although Averill advocates for ongoing, smaller transformation, she still stresses the need for big objectives. Executives, she explains, must have a strategic outcome to guide all the smaller transformational initiatives. “The companies that I see achieving success,” she adds, “still start with a real problem to solve for. They still understand where they want to be.”

What sweeping transformation still gets right

Not all IT leaders believe large-scale transformations are problematic. Marco Bill, senior vice president and CIO of Red Hat, is one of them.

“I think in some cases you need to do big ‘T’ transformation,” he says. “Sometimes you just have to go for the full heart surgery.”

Bill points to transformation of its go-to-market stack as case in point. After trying to transform it piecemeal and failing to get traction, Bill and his C-suite colleagues planned for a multiyear transformation that launched in 2022 with a dedicated team and a top-down mandate for change.

The approach delivered the clarity, resources, and heft the transformation required to succeed, he says. That in turn got regional managers onboard in a way they hadn’t been for prior attempts at small-scale transformation. It also enabled the dedicated teams to build and implement new technologies and reengineer processes without having to support the existing stack, which was supported by an existing IT team.

“We weren’t flying the plane and building a new one at the same time,” Bill says, noting that this facilitated faster delivery of business objectives, including lower costs and improved process speed.

Striking the right transformational balance

But despite his defense of big transformation programs, Bill doesn’t discount the value of more bite-size transformation efforts. There’s need for both, he says.

Jose Baeza, CIO of BMI Group, a Standard Industries company headquartered in the UK, agrees.

Baeza, who defines transformation “as those moments where we change our business model (i.e., how we do business) or our operating model (i.e., how we organize ourselves),” believes there is a place for major transformation.

He points to an ERP rollout as an example, noting that it’s “an essential platform reset that allows an organization to fundamentally rethink its business processes, operating models, and customer interactions.”

But he’s also “a firm believer in a culture of continuous evolution, where smaller, more manageable transformations lead to big transformations over time.” He notes that “organizations have a finite capacity for deep operational shifts. Running major transformations too often or simultaneously can lead to change fatigue, ultimately undermining scope, delivery, and long-term adoption.”

Like other IT leaders, Baeza believes small bets have big payoffs, with continuous evolution yielding large-scale transformations over time while providing other benefits along the way.

“By breaking big visions into iterative building blocks, you give your organization the ability to course-correct in real-time while using technology as a force multiplier for growth,” he explains.

He says CIOs today must be able to deliver both those types of transformation — the capital “T” ones as well as the smaller, incremental ones.

“Just as important as a major transformation is bringing excellence into the day-to-day — driving tool adoption, staying ahead of market shifts, and fostering a high-performance culture,” he adds. “Our role as technology leaders isn’t just delivering systems. It’s creating an ecosystem where continuous, day-to-day innovation can flourish.”

item.title: Ghost businesses are easier to build than ever
item.description:
Earlier this year, CBS News reporters set out to investigate 89 licensed hospice companies. The task was simpler than it seemed at first glance: state records tied these companies to a single, 32,000-square-foot Los Angeles building that also housed a salon, a law office and a modeling agency. The building’s owner said only 12 were still there. The gap between the business registry and on-the-ground reality was clearly a problem.

When I saw that story, I did what any curious technologist in my position would do; I started thinking about finding those ghost businesses automatically using modern data analysis techniques. I turned our tools loose on it.

Trulioo’s business data covers more than 100 million U.S. business records, and its value here is in how those records connect. Linking each company to its directors, addresses and owners turns a registry into a map. My team quickly found clusters and registration spikes that appeared to confirm what federal investigators had spent years documenting manually. Many of these providers have been billing Medicare for years and collecting federal tax dollars.

The CBS News story is not an isolated case, unique to Southern California hospice care. We need to understand it as a window into a fraudulent architecture that operates in many different forms across industries and states and around the world. While most of the conversation about synthetic fraud has centered on creating fake people, fake businesses are the quieter half of the same problem, and likely much more impactful from a financial fraud standpoint.

Catching ghost businesses

By the time federal authorities finished connecting the dots on California’s hospice crisis, they had charged 15 people across nine interconnected investigations and estimated $3.5 billion in Medicare fraud from Los Angeles County alone. One licensed physician was linked to 63 separate hospice facilities, billing Medicare more than $35 million in a single year. A couple with prior tax evasion convictions operated a hospice under their daughter’s name.

Every one of those entities was a registered business. Each had a listed director. Each had an address. By every measure a standard Know Your Business check evaluates, the companies were legitimate. And standard verification, which evaluates entities one at a time, is exactly the wrong tool for catching fraud that exists in the relationships between businesses.

The California hospice case is also instructive because it shows the deliberate nature of this particular fraud architecture. Ghost businesses, which are paper companies that exist to bill for services that may never be delivered, don’t advertise their fakeness. They register properly, build websites, list phone numbers in public directories, and size themselves strategically. They cluster geographically to exploit the gap between what regulators check and what they miss.

The pattern gives them away. In Los Angeles County, the number of hospice providers grew by more than 1,500% between 2010 and the state’s 2022 audit, which was six times the national average relative to the county’s elderly population. That spike was visible in the registration data, along with the clustering, the shared director relationships and the address density. None of those signals would show up in a single entity check.

When my team layered those signals against our data, the fraud patterns lit up the screens. Postal codes in Van Nuys, North Hollywood and Glendale emerged as hubs in the entity graph. In one zoomed subnetwork, three directors shared ownership across two hospices with nearly identical names. Invisible in any individual lookup. Obvious at the network level.

Uncovering shells within shells

Bad actors building fraudulent businesses don’t usually stop at one fake company. These criminals build entire networks of shell corporations whose beneficial owners are other shell corporations, registered across multiple jurisdictions, with legitimate-looking surface entities and illicit activity buried underneath.

This means the hardest task in detecting business fraud is finding the layered ownership structure specifically designed to defeat verification. We look beyond the owner of a single fraudulent business and consider whether that person also owns ten others clustered in the same postal code, registered in the same six-month window.

Finding those connections requires graph database technology, which lets us trace connections despite layers of obfuscation. When pulling on suspected shell company threads, we often find the same entity at the center of dozens of businesses that appear entirely unrelated from the outside.

This is the problem ultimate beneficial ownership discovery exists to solve: a registry that lists the owner-of-record. Tracing who actually stands behind a company, through layers of other companies, is what separates a legitimate business from a front.

This same pattern shows up on social media and online marketplaces. Shoppers can see this anytime they find a dozen listings for the same product, clearly from the same manufacturer, just with slightly different logos.

The challenge is that some of these listings are legitimate resellers, right alongside those that aren’t. The line between a fake seller and a ghost business is thinner than most people assume, and the underlying network structure is often identical.

Addressing the forward-looking problem

Most business verification is backward-looking. You check what a company has done, what its compliance record shows and what its registration history looks like. The blind spot is that very few people ask what it’s likely to do next. That ability to look ahead is predictive and possible with modern data techniques including machine learning and AI.

The hospice fraud rings operating in Los Angeles ran long after their entities passed initial registration checks. They kept billing taxpayer money as ownership shifted, new shells formed and directors spread to additional clusters.

Catching a ghost business at onboarding is one checkpoint. These operations stayed hidden because nobody looked again once registration cleared. Risk has to be assessed before you spend on verification, at onboarding, when you set a risk threshold, and continuously afterward. That means holding years of historical business information and tracking businesses in real time, with thousands going inactive each day while thousands of new ones appear. Observed over time and projected forward, that data has enabled us to build what amounts to an early warning system for business fraud. Each flag also has to hold up when a regulator asks why, with an auditable line from the decision back to the data behind it.

Emerging fraud patterns are still hard to catch before clusters become statistically visible, and attackers are using AI to cut the cost of building ghost businesses. That means more of them, registered more convincingly, across more jurisdictions. Defenders can use the same technology, but only if the underlying data is connected and current.

Most organizations still check one business at a time. The fraud they’re up against is built as a network, and detection needs to be built the same way.

item.title: Building AI-enabled cities starts with putting people first
item.description:
The cities getting the most out of AI aren’t just the ones adopting it fastest but those putting their residents first. These cities are seeing more than twice the return on their AI investments compared with their peers. This is according to ThoughtLab’s new global report, Building a People-First, AI-Powered City.

The research is based on a survey of 525 senior officials across 215 cities worldwide, alongside a review of 363 city AI plans. The report found a clear link between how cities approach AI and what they get in return. It also identified 37 AI leaders that combine technology with strong governance, workforce development, citizen engagement and human-centred design.

Mark Wittenburg, Raleigh’s CIO, participated in the study and was part of the report advisory board. He thinks AI may be changing how government functions, but the core purpose of government hasn’t changed at all. “Our job is to serve the people and put community first,” he says. “Whatever technology we bring in should enable the needs of the community, whether that’s public safety, transportation, or delivering clean water.”

Heart of the matter

Raleigh’s early use of AI was to advance its Vision Zero goals, a global initiative that aims to eliminate road deaths and serious traffic injuries, rather than simply reduce them.

“At the time, our transportation team was counting cars at intersections, but the data they gathered only captured how many cars moved through the intersection,” Wittenburg says. “It didn’t reveal any insights we could use to help reduce fatalities.”

Working with NVIDIA, Raleigh built ML models that analyze video footage from intersections, and detect things like stalled vehicles or water on the roadway.

“Instead of reacting to a call from the community, we’re being proactive,” he adds. “Moreover, we can now look at lane utilization and see the left turn lane is 95% subscribed. With this information, we can change the signal timing and test the impact of these adjustments.”

The next step is to go further, looking at near misses. Using advanced analytics and building a vision learning model, the city can hopefully prevent accidents. While near-miss data isn’t a reliable predictor of exactly where the next accident will happen, when combined with other transport data like crash records, traffic volumes, and vehicle speeds, it can help identify trends and address risks before they result in fatalities.

“Accidents don’t actually happen very often but near misses happen more often than you’d expect,” he says. “By analyzing actual accidents and near misses, we have more data points to work with and can make more accurate decisions.”

Sky’s the limit

Raleigh is also using AI for microclimate modelling. As part of a citizen science project, data was collected at different times of the day and in different places. This was compiled into a map to show where hotter zones in the city, called Urban Heat Islands (UHI), are located.

For example, on the hottest days, temperatures in neighborhoods with less green space can be up to 20 degrees higher than in shadier areas with more vegetation. These maps can help Raleigh prepare for and respond to extreme heat.

Band of agents

Additionally, Raleigh is using AI to streamline three areas of its municipal operations. Its gen-AI chatbot, Raleigh, helps employees easily find information across different departments. The city is now pairing this capability with Ral-E, an AI agent that handles IT help-desk tickets, communicates with employees through Teams or email, and resolves defined requests.

It’s also deploying Alli, a separate agent that autonomously handles simple help-desk tasks like password resets. “We’re getting positive results because the agent works 24/7, so if you need help after hours, you can get it,” he says. When these technologies are interacting with people, trust is critical. “Being transparent about when someone is interacting with an agent rather than a person is important,” Wittenburg says. “We also must be clear about what data we’re collecting and how we’re using it.”

Common purpose

Across all these examples, the focus may be different, but the desired outcome of making Raleigh a better place to live is the same. For Wittenburg, a people-first AI strategy is about starting small, testing, and then scaling. “We approach AI with a crawl, walk, run mentality,” he says “And maybe we stub our toe a few times along the way. This process sees us experimenting with low risk, internal stuff before we use it in ways that directly impact or directly interact with the community.”

While private-sector businesses prioritize ROI, the public sector has a different measure of success, he says. “As a city, it’s more of a value discussion,” he continues. “We’re always asking if a project will add value by making staff more efficient and effective, or if it’ll have a positive community impact. The technology should never be in the driver’s seat. It’s just an enabler that helps us add value to the people.”

item.title: AWS Nitro Sandboxes Put Each EKS Pod in Its Own MicroVM with One RuntimeClass Field
item.description:
AWS has launched Nitro Sandboxes, running each opted-in EKS pod, ECS task or EC2 workload in its own Firecracker microVM with a separate kernel, enabled by one runtimeClassName field at no extra charge. A confidential mode adds attestation-gated key release. The documentation lists the trade-offs: no GPU passthrough, at most five sandboxes per vCPU, and half the compute on SMT instances.

By Steef-Jan Wiggers

item.title: Your AI is smarter. Is your business still working the same way?
item.description:
AI is getting smarter at remarkable speed. Employees can draft, analyze, search and automate routine work faster than they could a year ago. Recent research on the state of AI shows organizations continuing to expand adoption across functions and use cases.

Yet in many organizations, the business still works the same way. The same work moves through the same systems, waits in the same queues and stops at the same approvals. AI speeds up a task, and the benefit disappears into a process designed for another era.

I see this from two vantage points. CDW works across thousands of customer environments, so we have a broad view of where AI creates value and where companies get stuck. I also help lead CDW’s own AI strategy and transformation. We have made AI assistants available to more than 14,000 coworkers, built more than 12,000 agents and started redesigning core workflows.

That experience has convinced me the CIO’s challenge has changed. It is no longer simply enabling access to AI. It is helping the business move quickly without creating fragmented technology, uncontrolled cost and risks that IT will ultimately have to manage.

Where the productivity gains get lost

Here is the pattern I keep seeing. A company gives employees AI. People use it to summarize documents, prepare analysis and draft recommendations. Employees report saving time. But business performance barely moves.

The reason is simple. Every task sits inside a larger workflow. An employee may finish one step faster, but the output still lands in the same queue and waits for the same sign-off. Another team may still re-enter it in a different system. The task got faster. The constraint just moved.

We saw the same thing inside CDW. Usage climbed quickly, but usage alone couldn’t tell us whether the business was performing better.

The task is not the real unit of business performance. The workflow is. In many organizations, the next phase of AI value creation will come from improving how work moves across the enterprise, not simply automating individual tasks.

Don’t automate the workflow you already have

Once leaders see the workflow as the constraint, they’re tempted to apply AI to every step. That instinct is often a mistake.

Many steps in a process were built around the limits of older technology or around organizational boundaries that no longer make sense. Others survive because no one has questioned them. Put AI into each of those steps and you get a faster version of a process that shouldn’t exist in its current form.

The better approach is to start with the business challenge, not the technology. Define the outcome that matters and work backward. Which steps still add value? Which can disappear? Then decide who, or what, should do the remaining work: conventional automation, an agent or a person who brings judgment and accountability.

Our experience building agents inside CDW has changed how I think about them. I used to see agents as more capable assistants. Now I am more interested in how they can move work forward. That is what creates the opportunity to remove steps, not just speed them up.

That experience has also made us pragmatic. Not every problem needs an agent. Sometimes a simple rule works better and costs less.

Don’t automate the workflow you have. Design a better one.

Employees create readiness. Business leaders create authority.

A redesigned workflow still has to run through people, and each group has a different job.

Employees experiment and surface opportunities. Hands-on use is how people learn what AI can and can’t do and where it can help. But employees can only change the tasks they control, not the handoffs before and after them.

Business leaders choose which workflows matter and own the outcomes. They have the authority to bring functions together. But a workflow designed from the top will struggle if the people running it have never used AI or don’t trust it.

Inside CDW, we need both: broad access so coworkers build fluency, and leadership focus on a few core workflows where redesign can change performance.

Neither scales, though, if every team has to solve for tools, data, security and cost on its own.

The CIO mandate: Build the enterprise AI foundation before workarounds take hold

The CIO doesn’t need to own every use case or redesign every workflow. The mandate is to build the enterprise AI foundation quickly enough, and make it useful enough, that business teams build on it rather than around it. It’s also increasingly reflected in the questions shaping CIO agendas as leaders balance AI opportunity with governance, operating models and business value.

That foundation combines approved AI tools, trusted data and business context, connections into enterprise applications and workflows, security and governance, and visibility into performance, cost and value. Many of these principles align with established guidance for managing AI risk at scale. It gives employees a safe way to experiment and business teams a repeatable way to scale what works.

Timing matters. Business teams won’t wait for IT. If the foundation isn’t there, they’ll find their own tools and build their own connections. AI adoption will continue, just out of sight. The CIO then inherits the result: fragmented data, duplicated spending, inconsistent governance, cyber risk and little visibility into what AI is doing across the company.

Usefulness matters just as much. A foundation that is too restrictive or hard to use drives people around it. One that works becomes the default, and each new agent or redesigned workflow can reuse the data, connections and controls already in place. That is how we are approaching it inside CDW.

Build the highway for AI transformation, or spend the next several years managing the risks created on the side roads.

Measure what changed

AI will keep getting more capable. The competitive difference will come from what companies are willing to change around it. The measure of that change isn’t how much AI a company has deployed. It’s whether the business performs better.

That is the standard we are applying inside CDW. It is also the standard I would encourage every CIO to use. Do not stop at licenses, usage or hours saved. Ask whether AI has changed an outcome the business cares about.

Does the company now work better?
